dataset_family: Hospital Nuestra Senora de Gracia, Zaragoza (Spain): consecutively screened geriatric-outpatient MCI series, recruited Jan 2020 to Aug 2021, 59 MCI (32 sMCI / 27 pMCI), 24-month follow-up; not a public or named cohort
method_family: Evidence type for VF-27: a continuous baseline depression scale (EURO-D, 0-12) compared between progressors and stable MCI in a small longitudinal clinical prognosis cohort, with regression models and an unsupervised disease-progression model (RPDPM) over the longitudinal scores. At the evidence level this is the same kind of analysis as P-647 (a baseline depression scale in a longitudinal MCI prognosis cohort); the paper's own primary method (DPM plus logistic regression) differs from P-647's Cox model
what_it_shows: In 59 oldest-old MCI outpatients, baseline EURO-D did not separate those who progressed to ICD-11 dementia within 24 months from those who stayed stable (3.0 +/- 2 vs 3.4 +/- 1.9; no p printed in a column that prints only p < 0.05; 37.5% vs 37% above the depression cut-off). The authors say that neither their regression models nor the disease-progression model supported depression as a predictor, and that EURO-D 'did not follow the progression towards dementia'. Chronic depressive disorders were not excluded, so the null is not produced by range restriction. There is no brain measure, and all participants have MCI.
why: Molina-Torres et al., Int Psychogeriatr 38 (2026) 100129. The PDF title and all eleven authors match the summaries.md block and the map entry. Against the Table A1 statement the study supports the conversion limb of the severity clause ('continuous severity scores fail to track ... conversion'): the study's own converter-versus-stable comparison of a continuous depression score is null, and the authors report that the regression and DPM analyses were also null. This is the same limb, and the same kind of evidence, that round 20 accepted from P-647, so it is marked 'yes' on the same standard. What it does NOT show: (a) the first clause, depression status associated with MCI, because every participant has MCI; (b) the brain-measures limb, because there is no imaging, and plasma p-tau181 (n = 47) is never related to EURO-D; (c) the 'although' clause about major-depression groups. Limits: small (27 progressors), so the null is low-powered; Table 1 prints no EURO-D p value (the column is headed 'P < 0.05' and blanks mean non-significant), and the regression coefficients for EURO-D are never printed; the DPM trajectory claim rests on the authors' sentence, because Fig. 3's caption does not list EURO-D and the figure is not in the extract; the outcome is all-cause ICD-11 dementia; Table 1 is internally inconsistent elsewhere (MMSE p = 0.039 in the table vs p = 0.02 in the text), which does not touch the EURO-D row. Independence: no shared sample, site or authors with P-643 (Korea University Guro, Seoul) or P-647 (Shanghai Brain Health Cohort). No shared sample or authors with the other candidates. The discussion cites Zuliani et al. 2021 (P-1326) only as literature. Method-family caution: its depression evidence is the same kind of analysis as P-647's, so if method family is judged by the analysis behind the supporting result rather than by the paper's primary method, it would not add a distinct method family.

quotes.quote: Chronic depressive disorders were not grounds for exclusion unless patients were experiencing a new active episode. Mild psychiatric disorders were allowed.
the EURO-D depression scale (scores from 0 to 12) [21]
Repeated-measures ANOVA compared longitudinal outcomes between pMCI and sMCI. Linear regression and binomial logistic regression served as predictive models.
After the three visits, 27 progressed to dementia (45.8 %, pMCI), and 32 remained stable (sMCI).

However, the p-tau181 marker shows limitations in reflecting the progression towards dementia, as individual trajectories are notably dispersed, nor did the EURO-D scale follow the progression towards dementia.

Regarding depression, it is remarkable that it affected 37.5 % of sMCI patients and 37 % of pMCI patients. The role of depression as a risk factor for dementia has been described in several studies in the literature [4]. Therefore, we might expect that depression in this study would be a predictor of progression from MCI to dementia, but neither the results of regression models, nor the scores of the proposed natural history of the disease support this conjecture.
we cannot rule out the possibility that specific symptoms of depression such as anhedonia might predict the progression [35], rather than a general screening.

Limitations, such as our small sample size, remain. A larger cohort, and thus a larger validation group, would help build a more robust DPM. There is also a high loss of patients to follow-up, close to 20 %.
